title: The Year Cicely Saunders Decided Her Hospice Would Not Be Exclusive
dek: In 1960 Cicely Saunders argued out what kind of place St Christopher's would be, chose a broad Christian foundation over a narrow one, and opened it in Sydenham seven years later.

story.event: Deciding in 1960 that St Christopher's would be an interdenominational foundation rather than an Anglican religious community, then opening it in Sydenham in 1967
story.summary: In 1960 Cicely Saunders, then researching pain at St Joseph's Hospice in Hackney, consulted friends and the theologian Olive Wyon on the character of her planned hospice, and by December decided it would be an interdenominational Christian foundation whose legal memorandum required only a chapel for Christian worship, setting aside the idea of a formal religious community. Supporters raised over £330,000, and St Christopher's Hospice in Sydenham admitted its first patient on 13 July 1967 and was officially opened on 24 July 1967.
paragraphs: On 4 March 1960 Cicely Saunders, a doctor researching pain at St Joseph's Hospice in Hackney, east London, wrote to Olive Wyon, a retired theologian in Cambridge, about a problem with her plan. The year before, she had circulated a ten-page document called The Scheme, setting out a modern home for the dying, by then named St Christopher's. Some people read it as a proposal for a new religious community. She was not sure that was what she meant.

She had come to the work through nursing and social work, then qualified as a doctor in 1957 to tackle the pain of people dying of cancer. In 1948 a dying patient, David Tasma, had left her £500 and the words "let me be a window in your home." At St Joseph's she was seeing what regular oral morphine could do, and the care of the Irish Sisters there, "something more than an ordinary group of professional women could ever give," she wrote.

Through 1960 she argued the question out in meetings and letters. A committed evangelical, she first leaned towards a Church of England foundation. Practical facts pressed too: the City Parochial Foundation, a large charitable funder showing interest, could not give to a purely Anglican venture. Rosetta Burch, an almoner in her circle, wrote that she was "a Christian doctor not a spiritual leader with a medical vision."

By December she had chosen. St Christopher's would be an interdenominational Christian foundation, and its legal memorandum would say only that "there shall be a chapel available for Christian worship." "I found that I just couldn't think it was right to be exclusive," she told Wyon. The idea of a formal community she set aside, writing that if they were to be drawn together, it would happen when they got there.

Seven more years of fundraising followed; supporters raised over £330,000. St Christopher's, in Sydenham in south London, admitted its first patient, Mrs Medhurst, on 13 July 1967, and Princess Alexandra opened it on 24 July. By the historian David Clark's account, every debt had been cleared by then. Saunders later said it took her "nineteen years to build the home round the window."

quote.text: There be also two false peaces, or unities: the one, when the peace is grounded, but upon an implicit ignorance; for all colors will agree in the dark: the other, when it is pieced up, upon a direct admission of contraries, in fundamental points.
quote.work: Essays, Civil and Moral (The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral)
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon, writing about quarrels between churches, warned against peace made by not looking closely, or by setting opposites side by side and calling it unity. Saunders settled the denomination question in one plain sentence and left the question of community open. Whether that was wisdom or postponement, the opening day does not say.

reflection: Saunders did not settle everything in 1960. She settled what had to be settled for the work to go forward, wrote it in a single sentence, and let the rest wait. A colleague's blunt letter helped her see which was which.

Whatever you are building, its character is still forming. Some questions about it, such as who it is for and what it will refuse, need an answer now; others can wait until there are people beside you to answer them with. Bacon's warning is worth keeping close: a question left open on purpose is not the same as one avoided because it is uncomfortable.
invitation: Write down one question about your work that you have been treating as urgent. Decide whether it truly needs an answer this month, or whether, like Saunders's question about community, it can be answered when you get there.

sources.supports: Saunders's first letter to Olive Wyon on 4 March 1960 and its wording about the Irish Sisters and the 'Community' question; The Scheme, a ten-page document circulated in the second half of 1959, and the name St Christopher's by the end of 1959; her evangelical orientation and initial preference for a Church of England foundation; the City Parochial Foundation's inability to fund a purely Anglican venture; Rosetta Burch's letter of 16 June 1960; the 6 December 1960 letter deciding on an interdenominational foundation, 'I found that I just couldn't think it was right to be exclusive', and the memorandum's chapel clause; setting aside the community idea, 'it will happen when we get there'.

sources.publisher: End of Life Studies, University of Glasgow (academic blog)
sources.supports: Nursing at St Thomas's, training as an almoner; David Tasma, a survivor of the Warsaw ghetto, dying in 1948 and leaving her £500 and 'let me be a window in your home'; studying medicine to work on the care of the dying; research at St Joseph's Hospice in Hackney from 1958; opening to first patients in summer 1967 in Sydenham as an independent charity; all debts cleared on opening day; 'it took me nineteen years to build the home round the window'.

sources.title: Our history
sources.supports: Supporters raised over £330,000; first patient, Mrs Medhurst, admitted on 13 July 1967; official opening by Princess Alexandra on 24 July 1967; three inpatient wards of 18 beds by 1968; home care from 1969.

sources.title: Dame Cicely Mary Strode Saunders (Inspiring Physicians)
sources.supports: Nurse, then almoner, then doctor (qualified 1957); David Tasma, a Polish refugee dying of cancer, left money towards a hospice; research at St Joseph's Hospice in Hackney showing what regular oral morphine could achieve; St Christopher's opened in 1967 as the first research and teaching hospice; her clarity that it was for people of all faiths or none.

sources.supports: Based on early-1960s correspondence: Saunders and her associates reconciled questions about the hospice's religious orientation, its relationship to medicine and its status as a community through a pragmatic turn.

cross_checks.claim: David Tasma left Saunders £500 and asked to be 'a window in your home'.

The decision: St Christopher's became a broad Christian foundation, with a chapel, rather than a narrowly denominational one or a religious community, and served people of all faiths or none.

Saunders qualified as a doctor in 1957 and showed at St Joseph's what regular doses of pain relief could do.

research_notes: Episode: the slate named the 1967 opening; the opening itself is documented mainly as dates, so the story centres on the documented decision of 1960 about the hospice's character (Clark, from Saunders's letters) and ends with the opening, keeping one continuous episode from decision to opening day. Bed numbers in The Scheme disagree: David Clark says a 60-bed home; the New York Times obituary says a 100-bed home; the story gives no figure. By 1968 St Christopher's ran three wards of 18 beds (St Christopher's), consistent with the 54 beds given in the BMJ obituary as summarised in search results (BMJ itself blocks automated requests and was not cited). Fundraising: St Christopher's says supporters raised over £330,000; no cited source gives a different total; Clark says all debts were cleared on opening day, which the story attributes to him. Timescales are framed differently: Clark speaks of eight years of fundraising and planning (from 1959) and Saunders of nineteen years (from Tasma's death in 1948); RCP and KCL say nearly 20 years; the story uses 'seven more years' from the end of 1960 and quotes Saunders's nineteen. Clark says she qualified at 38, RCP at 39 (born June 1918, qualified 1957); the story gives no age. The quoted letters (to Olive Wyon, 4 March and 6 December 1960; from Rosetta Burch, 16 June 1960) are quoted from Clark's blog, which reproduces them from the Saunders archive; ellipses in his excerpts were not crossed. The St Christopher's page sometimes drops automated connections but passed the source check. The New York Times obituary is cited from a reprint because nytimes.com blocks automated requests. Bacon's essay concerns unity among churches and is applied by analogy. Web search budget ran out during this entry, so a wider search for alternative fundraising totals was not possible.
